messages.content: i brought a book while waiting for my cousin, but i keep looking at the door instead of reading.
are you happy that they are coming, or worried that you might not see them come in?
i just want to see them. we have not met for a long time.
then you are thinking more about seeing your cousin than about the book. you do not need to make yourself read while you wait.
i am happy they are coming. say that part simply.
you are happy they are coming, and you want to see them as soon as they come in. the book can wait until another time.
say that with fewer words.
you want to see your cousin. the book can wait.
can you give me one simple thing to ask when they sit down?
how has your day been?
i would rather ask about the journey here.
then ask: how was your journey?
i wrote a story about a house with a garden on the roof. help me choose a name for the story from the words we have.
you could call it the garden above the house or the roof that grew. the first name says what is there. the other gives the roof a story of its own.
i like the roof that grew, but the roof itself does not grow. plants grow on it.
the roof does not grow in your story. the garden above the house is a clear name for what you wrote.
say that simply.
the garden above the house is a clear name for your story.
write a short first part where a child sees the garden for the first time.

a child walks down the street and sees flowers above a house. she stops and looks up. there is a whole garden on the roof, with a tree near a small table. she asks the person at the door how anyone gets up there.
should i answer that question right away?
you can, or you can let the child wait while the person gets a key. keeping the answer for a little while can give the next part a reason to happen.
i made one container of soup, then put some in another container. have i made more soup?
no. moving soup from one container into another does not add soup. you have changed where it is, not how much you made.
now there are two containers with soup in them. why is that not two meals for sure?
the number of containers does not tell us how much soup is in each one or how much a person will eat. two containers could each have only a little soup.
can one large container have enough for more people than two small containers?
yes, that is possible. to know, we need more detail about how much soup there is. the number of containers alone is not enough.
write a small conversation where someone looks at the food before asking more people to come.

we have soup in two containers. is it enough for our friends too? let us look at how much is in each container before asking them. one container has only a little. then we may need more food for the group.
say my last request in fewer words.
write a conversation about whether there is enough food for more people.
in my story, the child walks north to the library. the road is closed today. help me make the next part without saying the child can go through it.

the child stops when she sees that the road is closed. she looks at her map and goes back to the shop. a worker there knows another road to the library and can explain where to go. the child listens, then starts again by the other road.
say just the part about the worker helping her.
a worker at the shop gives her a different way to go. the child listens, then starts again by the other road.
did the story say the other road was shorter?
no. it only says that there is another road to the library. it could take more time or less time, but we have not chosen that detail.
make the other road longer so she gets to the library late.
the other road takes her past the park and around a large garden. she walks for longer than she wanted. when she gets to the library, her friend has already read the first part of their book.
ask my last request with fewer words.
make the other road take longer, so she is late.
can her friend still read with her?
yes. the friend can go back to the first part or tell her what happened before they read more together.
i want to ask my grandfather something at dinner that is not just how was your day.
you could ask: what did you enjoy doing when you were a child? that gives him a way to talk about a part of his life you may not know.
keep only the question.
what did you enjoy doing when you were a child?
he says he liked reading outside. i like that too. what can i ask next?
where did you like to sit when you read outside?
he says under a tree near school. can you help me keep the conversation going without choosing his answer?
you could ask what he liked to read or whether he read alone or with friends. those questions let him give the details himself.
ask just one of those.
did you read alone or with friends?
he says sometimes alone and sometimes with friends. write a reply about something we both enjoy.
i like reading outside too. it is nice to know we both enjoy that.
say his answer simply.
sometimes he read alone, and sometimes he read with friends.
write a story where a child learns that a parent does not know every answer, but can still help.

a child finds a word she does not understand in a book. her mother says that she does not know everything about that word either. the child asks whether they have to stop reading. her mother says no. they can look at the other words, think about what is happening in the story, and ask someone who knows more. together, they work out how the word is used on that page, even though they still have questions about the word itself.
tell the first part simply.
a child finds a word she does not understand in a book. her mother says that she does not know everything about that word either. they look at the page together to see what the story can tell them.
why is the mother still helping?
she is helping the child think, look at context, and choose what to ask next. helping does not always mean knowing every answer before the conversation starts.
what could the child ask a teacher later?
we found this word in a story and are not sure what it is doing here. could you explain it with another example?
does the story say the mother is wrong about everything?
no. it says that she has a question about one word. that does not tell us she is wrong about everything else.
i found something i wrote last month. i can see where my writing was wrong now, though i could not see it then.
that can be a useful way to see what you have learned. is there one sentence you would like to change first?
i can see where my writing was wrong. i want to make it better.
then you can use what you know now to make one part better. you do not have to change every line at once.
i wrote he go to school. i think it should be he goes to school.
yes. he goes to school is correct. you can say i go and they go, but he goes.
explain that with fewer words.
use goes with he: he goes to school.
should i keep the old page even though part of it was wrong?
you can keep it if you want to see how your writing changes. an old page can have something wrong in it and still be useful.
make that last idea simple.
an old page can have something wrong in it and still help you see what you have learned.
my friend read a page in less time than i did. does that mean they understood it better?
not from the time alone. knowing how long it took does not tell us everything about what they understood.
ask my question and answer simply.
did they understand it better? the time alone does not tell us.
what could we do to see what each of us understood?
you could each explain the page in your own words, answer questions about it, or give an example of the idea. those can tell you more than the time taken alone.
what if i remember fewer details but understand the general idea?
then you know something about the general meaning but may need to go back for some details. understanding a page can have more than one part.
say that part with general.
you may understand the general idea but can remember fewer details. those are different parts of what you got from the page.
say what i can do about the details.
you can return to the page for the details you need.
write a message to my sister and cousin. my sister should bring the book, and my cousin should bring the cups. each person needs a different request.
for my sister: please bring the book. for my cousin: please bring the cups.
write it as a short request for each person without giving either person a name.
for my sister: please bring the book. for my cousin: please bring the cups.
explain what i wanted simply.
you wanted one request for your sister and another for your cousin, with each person knowing what to bring.
now make one message saying i will bring the book and both of them should bring a cup each.
i will bring the book. please each bring one cup.
how many cups is that from the two people?
two cups: one from your sister and one from your cousin.
does my book count as a cup?
no. the book is a different object. there are two cups and one book in that plan.
i returned to the library but sat in a different room. can i say i went back to the same place?
yes. you went back to the same library, but sat in another room inside it. the library was the same place, while the room was different.
say it simply.
yes. it is the same library, with a different room inside it.
write a short story where the other room has less sound.

a woman goes back to the library after lunch. in the room she used before, a group is talking about a book. she wants to read by herself, so she goes into another room. that room is quiet, and she sits by a window with her book.
say what i asked for simply.
write a short story where the other room has less sound.
did she leave the library?
no. she moved from one room to another inside the library.
can the first group still be doing something useful?
yes. they may be learning from talking together. the room was just not what she wanted for her own reading.
picoboi, if you give a clear answer, does that always mean it is true?
no. a clear answer can still be wrong. you should check important information rather than thinking that a sentence must be true because it sounds sure.
can you help with a simple example?
yes. if you tell me that a book is on the desk, i should use that fact. if i later say it is on the shelf without any new information, that answer would not follow what you told me.
what should you do if i say the book moved?
i should use the new detail. if you say you moved it from the desk to the shelf, then it is on the shelf in the conversation now.
what if i only say i moved it and do not say where?
then i know it was moved, but i do not know its new place. i should ask where you put it instead of making up a place.
ask me that question.
where did you put the book?
under the chair.
then the book is under the chair now, from the information you just gave me.
make this into one sentence. my uncle went to a shop. he looked at a book in the window. he went inside and asked about it. i do not know if he bought it.
my uncle went into a shop to ask about a book he saw in the window, but i do not know if he bought it.
can you make it shorter without saying he bought it?
my uncle asked about a book at a shop, but i do not know if he bought it.
now leave out the part about what i know. keep only what he did.
my uncle asked about a book at a shop.
explain my last request simply.
you asked me to keep what your uncle did and leave out what you did not know.
does the short sentence still say he went inside?
not clearly. asking about a book at a shop could happen at the door or inside. the shorter sentence leaves out that detail.
add inside to make it clear.
my uncle went inside a shop and asked about a book.
